utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We will have the next witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud the affirmation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- that is on the card handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I believe Ms. Kravica has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, witness, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Saranda Bogujevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Ms. Bogujevci?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I was born in the town of Podujevo, Kosovo, 12th of June, 1985.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where are you currently residing?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: In England, Manchester.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in Manchester?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Since September 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In May 2000, did you provide a video interview to a representative of the OTP Simon Matthews in Manchester about events that you had witnessed in Podujevo in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you provide a second statement to representatives of the OTP in -- last year, October of 2008, regarding these same events?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review both the transcript of your video interview and your written statement?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please make a pause before asking the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Bogujevci, since we're both going to be speaking the same language today, we have to pause between question and answer in order to allow the court reporter to record the -- all what is being said here in court?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Having reviewed -- having recently had the opportunity to review both the transcript of your video interview and your previous statement, are you satisfied that the information contained in these documents is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I do -- I did see those some like names spelling mistakes, and things like that, but apart from that it's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the spelling mistakes are in which of the two documents, your previous statement or in the transcript of the interview?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: In the previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Sorry. I can't remember now which one it was. It was from the previous statement, just some of the names were spelled wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Other than that, are you satisfied that the information contained in these documents is true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender both of these documents these are C05128, that's the transcript of the video interview and C05127, this is the previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 01528 [sic], Your Honours, will be P00372 and the next one with the 65 ter number 05127 will be P00373.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Bogujevci, did you also testify about these same events that took place in Podujevo in March 1999 before the Belgrade district court in the trial against Sasa Cvjetan?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review the transcript of your testimony before the Belgrade court?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed it, if you were asked the same questions that you were asked during your testimony there, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this transcript into evidence. I do want to point out that this is 05129. We have uploaded a version in e-court which I have been told by my learned colleague from the Defence, it's incomplete, it's missing three paragraphs. It was missing those three paragraphs in the version that we received from the Belgrade court. My learned colleague has a different copy which is complete and it has that -- it was page 13 which was missing and which contained these additional three paragraphs. Unfortunately we don't have it at this stage. I only received this morning a translation for that, for the witness to review. So at this stage I seek to tender the version that is in e-court, but I do point out that it is missing a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see from signs of those who are always ahead of us in front of me that we have the additional paragraphs in hard copy, no doubt thanks to the assistance of Mr. Djurdjic. So we will receive those as part of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And what I'd propose is that -- I'm sorry. What I propose is that we will send this last bit for translation just so that it -- the whole testimony gets uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It will be received, the transcript and the additional page in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D00374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I will now proceed to read a brief summary of this witness's evidence. The witness is a survivor of a massacre that took place in the town of Podujevo, Kosovo, on 28th March, 1999. On the weeks preceding the commencement of the NATO bombing, there was an increase in police and military presence on the streets of Podujevo. Once the NATO bombing began, the witness and her extended family were staying in the family compound in Podujevo. Another family, the Duriqis were also staying in a house at the rear of the compound. On the 28th March, 1999, a police vehicle stopped outside the family compound. Fearing for their safety, the witness family moved to the house where the Duriqis were staying. At the time the family included only women and children as the men had gone into hiding. The witness describes how that day persons whom she describes as soldiers entered into the family compound and ordered the group out of the compound and into a neighbour's courtyard. Once in the courtyard the soldiers opened fire on the group killing 14 persons all women and children. The witness and four of her cousins survived the massacre. The witness also describes the killing of an elderly male member of the Duriqi. Family and of a neighbour. I would like to request for the usher to please provide the witness with a copy of her statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Bogujevci, I would like to move to your statement and to ask you a couple of questions about events you described in your statement of October 2008. Now, in paragraph 17 of your statement, you referred to the commencement of the NATO bombing, and you say in the weeks -- previous weeks and months before the NATO bombing, there had been a significant development and an increase in the number of policemen and army soldiers on the streets of Podujevo, and you say these were a regular sight. Was this something that you yourself saw, this increase in the number of police and soldiers on the streets of Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I can't remember the exact date, but I remember tanks going past my street and there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this something that happened on a specific day, or did you see this happen on different occasions, these tanks going by your street?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I particularly remember that -- that day on -- when the tanks -- but there was always, you know, soldiers around the town and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how many weeks prior to the commencement of the NATO bombing did you see these tanks going by your house?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure, but it could have been kind of the beginning of the year, so, you know, the beginning of 1999, roughly around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say in paragraph 19 that in days prior to the commencement of the NATO bombing, there had been rumours that Serb forces were targeting and killing men, and so the decision was made for your father and Selatin to hide away from the house. Do you recall how you received this information that Serb forces were targeting and killing men?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I just remember being -- everyone being at home, and I don't remember exactly who -- who said it, but I just heard that, you know, men were being targeted; and we asked for my father and my uncle to leave the house, especially my cousin Nora, she was really worried about my uncle. So she said to him, you know, please leave because we'll be all right because we're only women and children. And so we asked to leave -- we asked them to leave, but they were still around the town but they were just not staying at the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, turning to events that happened on the 28th of March, you say in paragraph 25 that you were alerted to the fact on the morning -- early morning of 28th March that someone had seen a police vehicle pull up in front of your compound and that you decided if -- because you feared for your safety, to move to your uncle's house in the rear of the compound. Why was it decided that you would be safer in your father's uncle's house at the rear of the compound?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It's just because my house is on the main street, so it's right by the street, and -- you know, my father's uncle's house is further inside, in the garden, so we thought, you know, maybe it would be safer to be away from the main street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 26 you indicate the persons who -- once you had moved to this house at the rear of the compound -- the persons who were staying in this house, and you referred to 19 persons, members of your family, the Bogujevcis, and members of the Duriqi family, and you also referred to two persons by the last name of Lugaliju, Nefise and Fezrije. Since when had these two persons been living with your family?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: They were with us for a while because they lived in the village and there was a lot more going on around the villages before the NATO bombings in the town, you know, you constantly hear, you know, like bombings and stuff like that from the villages. So she was with us for a while. I can't remember exactly when she came.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say there was a lot more going on in the villages, what exactly was happening in the villages?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, we just heard kind of, you know, explosions like, you know, bombs and stuff like that. So it was -- you could constantly hear it from the villages. So everyone was moving from the villages into the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand from your statement from this list of persons that you were 19 in total in this house in the rear of the compound, and that the only man in the group was a person by the name of Hamdi Duriqi, who was around 70 years old at the time?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, that's Enver Duriqi's father.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And for how long had the Duriqis been staying in this house at the rear of the compound?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were there for a few days, maybe two days or around, you know, just a few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why were they staying with you, the Duriqis?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Again, they moved, because they lived in the village so they just moved from the village into the town because, you know, they thought it would be safer to be in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you explain in your statement that in the early morning of the 28th, once you had moved to the house in the rear of the compound, you saw soldiers in the courtyard and you say there were approximately four or five of them moving around and then you decided to leave the house. Why was it decided that you should leave the house where you were, where the whole group was staying, once you saw these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, we were at the house and when our neighbours came and he said that it's better to stay in the house and then -- because the soldiers were coming into the houses and they were taking people out of the houses. So he said it's better to stay in the house; when they come in, they'll take you out. So we stayed in the house, and then from the other neighbour's house, which was next to the house where we were, my father's uncle's house, one of the soldiers broke a window that was -- you could see through to the garden where we -- to the house and the garden where we were. And then we saw them come in -- coming in, so, you know -- because we were told that they were taking them -- you know, they were taking everyone out of the houses so we started to going out to the houses because we thought they were doing the same thing. So we started walking out, and we were asked to raise our hands, and we had some bags with us like food and, you know, things like that, things that, you know, we needed. And they asked us if there was anyone in the house, and we told them there wasn't anyone in there, but they still went in to have a look. And they asked us to -- to drop our bags by the house. And then from there we were taken to our neighbour's house -- our neighbour's garden, sorry, and into the next neighbour's garden. But those that came in, they were around our garden and, moving forward towards our house and we were left with the soldiers on the other garden.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you also refer -- you also indicated that they searched you, and then they took your aunt, Shefkate, to a shed. Was this the same group of four or five soldiers who took your aunt to a shed?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, these soldiers -- they were other ones that we met at the other garden.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So there were two different groups of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. It's just -- the first ones, they just came in, took us out, then they moved forward and then we were taken to the other garden so there were other soldiers there. They were altogether but they were just moving into different places.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this first group of soldiers, with what type of uniform were they wearing if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: They had the green camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this second group of soldiers, with whom you were in the courtyard, were they wearing the same type or different?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us you were taken to a courtyard, and in your statement you indicate that you were then taken back out to the street?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: From our neighbour's garden we were taken to the next neighbour's garden; and then from that garden, we were taken out into the street where we saw the soldiers. But the soldiers on the street they had like mixed uniform, they had like the army trousers and like the police, they had all like mixed uniforms, and some of them had the same uniform as the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the group that was taken back out from the courtyard back out into the street, was this the same group of 19 people that were originally in the house?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, my auntie was separated, and we were in the other neighbour's garden and then we were taken to the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us that at the street -- once you were in the street, you were able to observe soldiers in mixed uniform. What else, if anything, were you able to observe while you were -- your group was out on the street?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, they were breaking the windows and the shops on the streets, and they were shouting at us and swearing, and there was constant shouting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did your group then remain together during this time that you were on the street?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, we were kind of in a line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any other civilians on the street while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Sorry, could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any other civilians on the street while your group was there?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: While I was taken out I saw Selman Gashi who was my mother's uncle. He was with another soldier and the soldier took his hats, the plis, the traditional Albanian hat, and they were teasing him and playing around with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what happened to Selman Gashi?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, he was taken into one of the shops, and then there was this other soldiers who -- this other soldier who was talking to Hamdi Duriqi and -- I don't know what he said to him, and then he slapped him on the face and then he took Hamdi into the shop where Selman was taken. And then the same soldier went in after him and we just -- we heard two, two gun-shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you seen Selman Gashi or Hamdi Duriqi since that day?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, where were you taken once -- from the street? You said you remained in the street, and then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: We were taken back to our neighbour's garden and we were -- when we were taken back, that's when I saw my auntie Shefkate, and she was crying. And as I said before, I -- the only thing I could understand that she was saying is that, you know, they were only children. And then from there soldiers took her behind the house, and we were taken as well behind the house. There was kind of like a small path and the soldier, he -- he just pushed her and shot her. And then I remember my cousins crying and, you know, calling, you know, mom. And then when I looked back at my auntie, she was on the ground, and then the soldier shot her again, and then he changed his gun, and he started shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to play a small video, which is 05219. And it's going to appear on your screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the garden.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could pause it there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken behind the house there, and my auntie was behind this path, probably around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can't see you --

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: You can't see it -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Don't worry, we'll see that later.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know when these images were filmed, the ones that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, 2004/2003, I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we -- is that you on that movie there?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We saw you entering a hallway. Where are you coming from?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: From the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this is the street where the group had been?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We saw you turn here and you go into this courtyard. Is this the courtyard that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You were telling us that the soldier shot your mother and then -- your aunt, and then he changed his gun and shot at the group. What happened when he began shooting at the group?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: When he started shooting, I just leaned on the wall and just slided down and then it hit me on my right leg, the bullets, and then after a while the shooting stopped; and there was a sound from someone, the kind of sound where you're struggling to breathe, and then the shooting started again. And then when the shooting started again, it hit me in my arm and in my back. And then after a while, the shooting stopped, and then it was quiet, so I wasn't sure whether the soldiers were still there or had gone. And then I decided to lift my head up. And then I just -- I looked around and I saw my cousin Genc, who had lifted his head up as well, and I saw my brother Shpetim, who was 9 years old. He was lying face-down on my feet, and he was shot on his head, half of his head was missing. And I also saw Fatos, my cousin Fatos, he was in front of me and there was something behind his back and it looked kind of -- it was something from the inside of the body, something from the body. So I thought the, you know, he was dead, but then he lifted his head up as well and I realised then that he was alive. And I also saw Enver's son, the old one, and he was shot in his face. I couldn't really tell where his eyes was or his mouth. And I also saw my grandmother, she was lying down, and she was facing me, and her eyes were opened. And then after a while I heard some sounds, and I said to Genc, you know, to lie down and I -- I lied down as well. And I heard, you know, voices, you know, talking. And then I also heard one of my cousins like -- you know, as a moan when you're in pain, and then decided to, you know, to move. I wasn't quite sure what was happening, but kind of as an instinct, I just -- I moved and then there were other soldiers in the garden, and they pulled me from the bodies and -- but they had a different uniform to the other soldiers, and they were speaking in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I may stop you there. How many soldiers did you see shooting at the group?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there in the garden or was there only one soldier in the garden?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, there were a few soldiers and there were soldiers always, you know, constantly moving, you know, coming in the garden, going out, you know but there were a few of them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You tell us in your statement that you believed that there was more than one soldier doing the shooting. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It's -- it's just with my -- with my wounds. The soldier that started shooting was on my left. When I slided down and I was on the ground, there was a wall in front of me, and there was a wall on to my right, where I was leaning on, and the soldier who started shooting was on my left, and I have a bullet wound which is -- on my back, which is a straight -- so I can't see how a bullet from my left can go straight, you know, onto my back. So that's why I believe there was more than one that did the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this was at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you just pause, please, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the witness was asked today by my learned friend, Ms. Kravetz, that only -- she answered that only one soldier opened fire on two occasions, and then she was taken back to her statement where she had stated that several soldiers had fired shots. I think that this was impermissible leading of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's partly the product of the system of using written statement supplemented by oral, Mr. Djurdjic. It's a matter which the Chamber will be well aware of and will assess in considering the whole of the evidence, but the statement did, as I understand it, specifically refer to more than one soldier as a matter of belief rather than a matter of observation. And so I believe Ms. Kravetz was correct in trying to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And then I should have stated, Your Honour, that this is at paragraph 60 of the statement. I failed to indicate that when I was putting my question. I would like to tender this clip, this video into evidence at this stage this is 05219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you tendering the lot or merely the moment that we have scene?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm tendering the whole exhibit. We're going to be seeing some still shots from the same video which I plan now to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long is the video?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The video, I believe, is approximately 45 minutes, maybe a bit longer, and it contains other images that we will be seeing. The reason I'm tendering the whole video is simply to provide some context to Your Honours of the location where the shooting took place. What we're interested in are the -- all the aerial shots and the shots of the garden itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think we better know more about what's in it, so perhaps you could return to tendering it when you have completed dealing with the video with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's no problem, Your Honour. If we could have 05219.01 on the screen, and I just want page 1 of that exhibit to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Bogujevci, we're going to be looking at some photographs on the screen that's right before you. I don't know if that has appeared. Do you recognise the photograph that is before you?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It's the garden where the shooting happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If the usher could kindly assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to -- there's a pen on the side of your screen, and I'm going to ask you to draw on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like you to mark with an X the location where the group was in the garden when the shooting occurred.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you put a 1 to indicate the shooter that you saw, the soldier that you saw shooting.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where you remember him standing.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I remember him standing around there, on the path.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you had indicated earlier that you also saw your aunt, Shefkate, and that she was shot. Could you put a 2 to indicate approximately where you recall she was standing before she was shoot.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Right next to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, I indicate that the witness has drawn a 1 and right above it a number 2. It's not very clear on the photograph, so I'm just indicating that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that there were other soldiers in the courtyard. Could you indicate where they were. You could simply just draw a line to indicate where they were.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Around there, like ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness has drawn a line right below the number 1 to indicate where other soldiers were standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, do we see -- in the video-clip we played earlier, we saw you entering through a passageway. Is that -- can we see this on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you indicate an arrow to show how you entered this courtyard, the direction from where you came.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see another courtyard right to the right of where you've drawn the arrow. Is this the courtyard from where you were originally brought, or is this a different house?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: This is the garden where I was when my aunt Shefkate was separated from us, and we were taken to the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this is the garden we see to the right of where you've drawn the arrow?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we don't see a street on this photograph, but where would the street be on this photograph. If you could draw a line to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It would be around, behind the house. I don't know how to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So it would be --

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Because we were -- so you went through there and then you take -- it goes straight into the -- into the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the arrow that you've drawn, the street would be behind the entrance we see there where the arrow starts?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could this photograph be assigned an exhibit number before I move to the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibits we've received this morning, we've noticed -- the court officer have noticed have been given a wrong number. So I'd ask him to re-assign the numbers now for those exhibits, and we'll also receive this photo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. 65 ter number 05127 was assigned P00373; 65 ter number 05129 was assigned P00374; and 05128 would be assigned P00375; and the photograph with the markings the witness has just made with 65 ter number 05129.01 would be assigned P00376.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we could see page 2 of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, Ms. Bogujevci?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes. It's still the garden where the shooting happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In paragraph 39 of your statement you say that when you were taken out to the street from this courtyard, the first time you were taken out, you were taken to a street facing the police station. I would like to know, is the police station visible in this photograph; and if it is, if you could draw a circle.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: As far as I can make out in the picture, that would be the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I wonder if this photograph could be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have page 3 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It's the place where we were and -- when we got shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you draw an X to show -- indicate where it was that you were standing when the shooting occurred.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I was kind of in the middle -- kind of in the middle of everyone, really, of the wall, so probably around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you had indicated earlier that when the shooting started you slid down the wall. Were you referring to this wall that may have just marked?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where would the shooter have been standing in with regard to --

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Further -- further away on -- to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If this photograph could please be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00378, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could see page 5 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is shown here on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: That would be the wall that was in front of me that I was facing when I was down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that this wall has markings that have been covered. Were those there on the day of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So would those have been caused by -- on the day of the shooting, those markings?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, on the day of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now see page 6 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise the persons on this photograph, Ms. Bogujevci?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, it's my mother, Sala, and my father, Safet Bogujevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was your mother in the group that was shot in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what happened to your mother?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: She was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How old was your mother at the time --

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: She was 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we see the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It's my grandmother, Shehide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was your grandmother in the group in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What happened to your grandmother?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: She was killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how old she was at the time?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Around 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now could we see the last photograph of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise the two persons in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, on the right is my older brother, Shpend Bogujevci, who was 12 years old at that time, who was also killed; and to the left is my brother, Shpetim Bogujevci, who was 9 at the time, who was also killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this video-clip that we've seen and these images, you've told us that they were shot -- that they were filmed approximately in 2003/2004. Do you recall who filmed these images?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, it was a journalist, Paresh Patel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And from which agency was this journalist?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: The BBC.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know what was done with these images that were filmed that day, the video that was filmed?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: There was a documentary that was shown in England.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was that documentary about?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It was about the story of what happened to our family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what that documentary was called?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It's part of a programme that was in BBC called Real Story.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And approximately do you recall when that documentary was aired, the Real Stories?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was around the -- towards the end of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender both the still shots and the clip that we played or the video that was played earlier. These are 05219 and 05219.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Photos and the video will be received. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, but are we admitting only the clip that we saw or the part of the film that we did not see as well? Ms. Kravetz showed us, as far as I can remember, I'm not sure now, only the wall by the building and the entrance into the yard, the witness entering the yard. I think that's about 4 seconds, and we didn't see more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you object to the tendering of the whole video?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. We did not see --or, rather, now we see that the witness confirmed the name of the author, the name of the film, and the time; but we did not see any of that ourselves. The witness confirmed only the part that -- I mean, that has to do with when she walked in, and I'm not objecting to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the images that we just saw are all from the same video. The reason I -- as I indicated earlier that we are seeking to tender the whole video is to provide Your Honours with some context of what this courtyard looks like, from where the persons were brought into the courtyard, and the adjoining buildings. So we have taken these shots from there, but there is more footage in the video that shows -- that will provide Your Honours with a better idea of what the location looks like. Due to time constraints, I'm not able to play further clips from the video, and so that's why we've prepared these still shots, in order to proceed faster with this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The objection is made simply on the basis that it hasn't been viewed in court, Ms. Kravetz. Have you got something to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, the video has been provided to the Defence. We provided it when we received it from the BBC in November of last year, so I imagine my learned colleague has had the opportunity to view it fully. I don't know if the objection is to a specific portion of the video, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The objection made is that it hasn't been viewed in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, Your Honours, we saw a portion of it, a small clip of the video, and I'm unable to play the remainder of the video simply due to time constraints because it is a lengthy video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will come back to this matter after we've had cross-examination, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, there are the photos which will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photographs under 05219.01, Your Honours, would be assigned P00379.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Ms. Bogujevci, just very briefly, you were telling us that you were -- you sustained several injuries during the shooting. Can you tell us exactly where you were injured in this incident?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: My right leg, my left arm, and my back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how many gun-shot wounds did you sustain in total?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: There was two in my leg and there was one in my back and in the whole of my arm, my left arm, and my hands, the whole of my arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how many gun-shot wounds did you receive in your left arm?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: As a result of the injuries that you sustained, today do you have any sort of complications with using your left arm?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I have limited movement and I can't straighten my fingers or make a grip; also with my elbow, I can't straighten it fully or kind of bend it as well, you know, to be able to -- you know, to reach anything. So I have very limited movements in my arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just going briefly back to the events of the 28th of March, in total how many persons were killed in the courtyard that we saw there on this video?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: My mother, my two brothers, my grandmother, and my aunt Shefkate, and my cousin Nora, my father's auntie, Nefise, and her daughter-in-law. So it's eight members of my family and also the seven members of the Duriqi family and Selman Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who survived the killing?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: My cousin Fatos, my cousin Jehona, Lirije, and Genc, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you describe how you were taken to the hospital in Pristina and that at some point your father came to visit you. How did your father find out that you were at the Pristina hospital?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Jehona's -- one of Jehona's classmates was at the hospital before the NATO bombing started, so his father wasn't able to get him out of the hospital straight away. So later on he came to -- you know, to take him, and he knew my father, and I told him what had happened, and he said that he will try and find him and tell him where we were and what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was he able to locate your father?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes. After -- after, you know, what happened, I think it was about after a month my father came to see us at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did you remain at the hospital in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I was there until June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where did you go once you left the hospital in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I was at home, but also there was some doctors with the NATO, the KFOR, that came at Kosovo who were changing our bandages. And after that, in September, we were flown to England, to Manchester, to have medical treatments there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did you continue your medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: For quite a few years. I mean, I still sometimes have to go for physiotherapy because my fingers, sometimes they get stiffer. So I still, you know, sometimes go to the physiotherapy, and I see my doctor as well still.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Saranda, my name is Veljko Djurdjic, and I'm a member of the Defence team of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. Together with me today is also Ms. Marie O'Leary, and the lead counsel is away on official business. His name is Dragoljub Djordjevic. Before I put some questions to you, I would like to express my deepest and most sincere condolences due to the loss of your nearest and dearest and the kind of pain that can never go away. I wish to say to you that I would not be putting a single question to you had the Office of the Prosecutor not taken a statement in October 2008, the one that they are using now. I believe that defence of accused persons is one of the basic postulates of criminal proceedings; however, since the statements you gave and the interview you gave in 2000, and in the proceedings in 2003 before the Belgrade district court, since all of these documents seem to be insufficient, I am compelled to take you back to the time you most certainly wish to forget and to put a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I start with my questions, I would like to draw your attention to a particular matter. We have admitted into evidence the transcript from the hearing held in Belgrade on the 9th and 10th of July, 2003, K --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot follow the numbers at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Djurdjic, you're referring to what is now Exhibit P375, the transcript of the proceedings in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. It says 375 here, yes. So these are 38 pages that we have admitted. I would just like to indicate that on the 10th of July, at the very beginning, Bogujevci, Fatos, the witness's cousin, made a statement; and the witness's statement is from page 8 through 13, the one that I found in the documentation that I received from the Belgrade court. So from page 1 to 13 we have the witness statements at the main hearing that was held there, and those are the people who testify here too. I believe that that is the only portion that should be admitted into evidence because these are two witnesses that we are hearing over here. As for the 9th of July, after page 13 -- I mean after the witness's statement, I mean Ms. Saranda's statement, that is not relevant for these proceedings because these witnesses will not be showing up here. So that's the only thing I wish to indicate at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If there 's been any misunderstanding, the only exhibit that the Chamber intended was the transcript of the evidence of this witness in the proceedings in Belgrade, and if there has been some more extensive transcript included, that will not form part of our exhibit. It is the evidence of this witness given in Belgrade which, for this purpose, becomes part of the 92 ter admitted evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I may add, Your Honour, we've only uploaded the portion that refers to this witness, and in the English we've redacted the paragraph that is -- precedes her testimony and the one that continues in order to only have that portion in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So I think your concern, you needn't worry about that, Mr. Djurdjic. We only have the transcript of the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I said this because this is the document that I received, 38 pages long. So I wish to indicate that to you. If matters are clear, then I think that we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Saranda, could you please tell me, when was your memory the best, when you first made your statement in Manchester, or at the trial in Belgrade in 2003, or in October last year?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, my memory's clear of what happened, you know, even now -- you know, of course in 2000 and 2003 it was closer to the time, and now it has passed -- some time has passed, but that doesn't mean that I forgot things that happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Saranda, we are not bringing into question what you are testifying about; however, in your statement from October 2008 there are many new things that you had not spoken about before that. That is why I wish to clarify certain matters. As for the actual event, incident, what you've been repeating all along, I really am not going to put any questions to you. What grade were you in March 1999 at school?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I was on year 8, just the end of high school, in the Kosovan way, the way the system was there at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said the system was organised there. Was this a special organisation or were these schools that were attended by all?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, no, the -- I mean, I don't know how the system was. You know, I -- I was a kid at that time and I never questioned it. But we -- there were separate schools. There were the schools where just the Albanians went and there were schools where the Serbians went. The school that I was actually supposed to go to was taken away from us, so we had to go to another school, and that -- that school that was taken was made especially for Serbian kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, when was this school taken away, as you had put it? Did you ever attend that particular school?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, when I started my first year, so I was around 6 years old. I remember just before starting school going there, and then after that, that's when it was taken away and we had to attend this other school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where was this other school?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: The one -- there's -- on the first -- from year 1 to year 4 we were moved to a smaller school which was supposed to be kind of like, you know, kindergarten school, there was that kind of age, and it's in -- it's in the main part of the town where the river -- the river is. It's close to the town hall. And then from that school, after I finished year four, we were moved to another school so that other kids could use the other school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, the building where you were up to year 4, whose house was that? What was that house?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, that was a school. It was like a, you know, for kids who go to those schools before they start the first year. So, you know -- I don't know, like a nursery, but it was -- it was a school. It wasn't anyone's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, that's the kindergarten. But when you started school, could you please tell me where was that building and who did that building belong to when you started school, year 1?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: The building was, as I said, close to the river, which is the main part of the town. As to who the building was run by, I don't know. I never questioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who your teacher was?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me your teacher's name and was that the teacher of all the children who attended that school?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, her name was Fatima, and she was the teacher who had my class and there was other teachers who had other classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I understood things correctly, it was a mono-ethnic school, the one that you attended?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there any children at that school that belonged to other ethnic groups apart from the Albanian ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, it was just Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was any other language spoken at the school, apart from Albanian?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, it was just Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how that school was financed?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, I was a kid, you know, I never questioned it, how it was financed. That didn't really interest me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you said to me that the school was in that building. Was the school there before you started school, before you started year 1; and how was it that you knew that the school was there?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, the school was already there. But, as I said, that school was used for children before starting the first year. But because the other school had been taken away, so that was the only option that we had, that was the only school that we could go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, where was the other school then?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: The other school is -- I don't know how to describe it. It's -- the other school that was supposed to be like a secondary school. So the -- I don't know how to describe it really. As from the main town and there's another main street where my house is, so the school's further up past my house, so further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was this a public building, the one that you attended school at?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, there were two buildings. We were only allowed to use one of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the other building there were other children who went to school in a different shift; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, the other building, that was empty. That wasn't used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what the name of the street that you lived in was?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: At that time it was called Kosancic Ivana.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You first said that in October 2008 when you made your statement then. How did you find out that that was the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Because I used to live around the street, and I must have asked my parents or -- I don't know, I don't exactly remember how I found out that was the street, but I used to live in that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly you lived there, but in 2000, when you gave that interview, you didn't know the name of the street. You knew the new name of the street because you were visiting Podujevo with some other people.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: So maybe I must have asked my father how the street was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that Enver Duriqi's family came to stay with you because of the conflict that the KLA had with the army and police in the village?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. All I knew was that he came to the town because there was a lot more danger around the villages. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Of course, I've -- I did hear about them, so I knew they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what they did and how they operated and where they operated?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No. You know, I was a child at that time, so really -- you know, information like that wouldn't really be given to me and I don't really know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm absolutely certain of that; however, I do have to ask you about paragraph 16 of your statement, dated the 7th of October, 2008. It says here: "A short time before the commencement of the NATO air campaign, the family of Enver Duriqi, a friend of my father, moved into the third house in our compound because they felt that their lives were threatened in their home village Obranqa, in Podujevo Municipality, where fighting had broken out between the KLA and Serbian forces."

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I don't actually remember ever saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Saranda.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I don't think I ever said anything about that because I don't know anything about that. I know there was -- as I said, there was bombings and, you know, it was said that it was -- you know, a lot more were going on in the villages, but -- you know, I never said that I -- it was between KLA or, you know, the Serbian forces. I just said that they came into the town because they thought that their lives were in a lot of danger there, but not necessarily that there was these fightings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the problem, Ms. Saranda. This statement, as it is written here - and you said at the beginning of our hearing today that you accept it as your own, as the truth, and nothing but the truth - and this is what has been written into evidence --

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Can I see the part that you're referring to. Which number was it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Of course. In English it is page -- paragraph 16. The English version is page 3, paragraph 16. You can read it of course.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember actually saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that these were not your words and that this is not something that you had said yourself?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I don't remember saying specifically that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you know from the Serb community in Podujevo at that time? All my questions addressed to you today have to do with that period of time. If I'm going to ask you anything outside that period of time, I will specifically say so.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: There were some of our neighbours that I knew, and one of them used to work at the hospital as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it one single person that you knew who was an ethnic Serb --

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Just a family that I knew, but the lady, I knew her more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, you say here in your statement that relations between the Albanians and Serb families at the time, I mean -- well, were very good. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, we were fine with our neighbours. We didn't have any problems. We spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. With one family, right?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that's the family I knew. I think my family knew other people, but that's the ones I saw the most and knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. One family then. Thank you. Do you know when the NATO air campaign started in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: It was in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the date?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the targets involved were, what targets were engaged by NATO when the war started? In your statement, in paragraph 17, you say, and I quote: "On the 24th of March, 1999, NATO commenced an air campaign in Serbia, involving the bombing of certain targets throughout the country, including Kosovo." Are those your words, Ms. Saranda?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Sorry, I misunderstood the question. I thought you were asking something more specific than that. So, yeah, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me then, what were these certain targets that NATO was supposed to bomb that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know the specific targets that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm asking you whether this is your own sentence or not, since this statement was made and has been admitted into evidence, that NATO has certain targets that were bombed throughout the country, including Kosovo. If you said that, could you please tell me what the certain targets were; and if you did not say this, then please say that you did not say it.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, you know, either NATO was bombing Yugoslavia, so that included obviously Kosovo, but I don't know specific targets of, you know, where the bombings were. You know, I didn't know they were going to bomb this or they were going to bomb that. I know, you know, I know that they were bombing the -- as Yugoslavia, but I didn't know, like, specific targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Although you've already explained this, in paragraph 17 you say that on one particular day you saw a column of tanks going through town. Did I understand you correctly when you were answering Ms. Kravetz's questions today?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Saranda, could you please tell me whether you make a distinction between the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, the police used to have the blue uniform, so when the -- from -- the way I understood, it was the army who would have the camouflage and so -- but the police used to have the blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in paragraph 18 you say that: "In the weeks building up to the NATO air campaign, many ... families started to move into ... Podujevo ..." Tell me -- actually, further on it says that: " ... Serbian forces had been burning houses and killing people in the villages." Tell me, you had heard about that from someone, right, this is not your very own knowledge, what you say in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, and there was -- that was on the news all the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the news that you were watching?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: From what -- I can't remember really which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but I think that the time would be right for the technical break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if you feel you need to continue after the break, we -- is that the case? You have more to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I have about 10 or 15 minutes, not more than that, Your Hounour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we will, I think, have the break now. The witness has been here for an hour and a half and would appreciate it; and we will resume at 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bogujevci, can we continue, please. Am I right if I say that after the NATO air-strikes began there was no water and electricity in Podujevo anymore?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes. The electricity sometimes would come on just for a little bit and then it would go off again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And electricity would come and go for all the inhabitants of the town; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I think so. I mean, once the NATO bombing started we were inside of the house, so we didn't go out to see other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that you don't speak or understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No -- I used to know like a few words, like -- but not actually speak it or understand it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that fortunately you could use what little you knew when you were hospitalised in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yes, also because I was there for three months so, you know, I picked up on some of the words that the nurses would use.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 25 you say that a police car stopped in front of your house. Could you please tell me, how were you able to tell that it is a police car, and could you describe it for me, please.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I have it in my notes that it's paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: All right. Well, it was described as a police car, so in Albanian they said autoblinda, so it's a police car. But I didn't see the car. I was told that the car stopped in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bogujevci. And do you know what an AK-47 is?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you learn that, could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. But when I described as it looked from the guy who started shooting at us, then I was told that it was an AK-47, but I can't remember exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to state then that these were not your words but that this was stated, but do you know at all what automatic weapons are?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, but not, like, specifically with names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you use expert terms, technical terms, like that in your everyday speech, automatic weapons or so, or did somebody rephrase your words, what you actually went to say? Was it put into words by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Not that -- I described the gun, and from my description that was an AK-47, so I learned that it was an AK-47. So I know that that's the gun now, but I don't know the other kinds exactly, all the names that they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's quite sufficient. Thank you. Am I right when I say that this terrible event lasted for a short time and that you received medical treatment immediately?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, after the shooting, as I said, after I got up and I saw my family and then when the other soldiers that came in with -- they had the different uniform, and they took my cousins and I to the hospital in Pristina. So I was in the hospital until June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention a person who assisted you. Did you learn that this was a physician who was a police doctor? I think you mentioned that he had a blue overcoat. I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The person who assisted you, who was first at your side. Do you know that this was a police doctor; or if you didn't know that at that time, was it something that you learned subsequently?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No. The soldiers that took us to the hospital, I don't know anything about them. I didn't know whether they were any doctors -- so I didn't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, do you remember a person wearing a blue overcoat that actually assisted you or aided you?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I just remember the -- there were, I think, two guys who pulled me out from the bodies, and they had the uniform. At this present in time I can't remember anyone with a blue coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember a blue vehicle that was the first vehicle that you were brought to?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know the outside of the vehicle, but from the inside of the vehicle it just looked like kind of the -- an army kind of ambulance probably because of the -- there was some medication in the car, so I just assumed it was a, you know, some sort of ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, well that was my next question, but I didn't really understand this properly. I read several of your statements. You were first taken to a vehicle, which was a police vehicle, and you said it was blue; and then you were transported in this car that you now told us about.

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I was -- I was sent straight into one of the vehicles. If I could see, please, where -- from where you're referring to the blue vehicle. I was only sent into the one vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn that this terrible event was the only event of that kind that happened in this short period of time in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Well, at that time I didn't really know what was happening, but afterwards -- I mean, I -- there were other people who died and -- friends of mine, but they didn't die in Podujevo, so I don't -- I don't remember really -- at this time I don't remember if there were any other massacres that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right and did you learn that the on-site investigation team from the police immediately went to the scene, as did the investigating judge who carried out the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that this is something that you learned subsequently over the course of the years that a crime-scene investigation team of the police went immediately to the crime scene, as did the investigating, and that an on-site investigation was carried out and there was a photo file produced containing a number of photographs of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that they went immediately after it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the interpretation is correct. It's not whether they went or -- but whether they came. Did you learn --

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Oh, no, I don't know whether anyone went -- went in after it happened. I don't know if I understand the question right, but as far as I -- but I don't know of anyone that went in after it happened and took -- did the investigation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me try and rephrase the question. In the course of the trial in Belgrade, were you shown a photo file from the crime scene, the investigation report, and other documents produced that pertained to the event that you testified about, and then carried out the identification?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I remember carrying out the identification. I can't remember seeing any pictures of -- after it happened at this moment. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that a sketch was made of the scene, what you showed us today on the photographs, that there was a sketch, an outline, of the compound?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: I don't -- at this moment in time, I don't remember seeing the sketch at the trial there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, you do have your medical records about the injuries that you had sustained?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Yeah, there's medical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a record from the Pristina Hospital and the documents that you got in Manchester, UK; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: And there's definitely documents from Manchester, but I'm not too sure whether there are any documents from -- from Pristina. I'm not too sure about that. But there are documents -- there are records from Manchester.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you hand over the medical records to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: At the -- I'm not too sure at that time if -- if I did send any. It's just because these things usually would go through the contact with the doctor, so I'm not too sure if they did take any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that no medical records were shown to you today about your injuries and the course of treatment and your current health?

utterances.speaker: SARANDA BOGUJEVCI
utterances.text: Not today, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bogujevci. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. This completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
